rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is the most progressive destination in the region for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, the international airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition. Every foreign visitor transits this airport, making it a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Foreign anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing governing coalition and the war aftermath have weakened protections, though a national security committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
rewrites.blindTangential: Dating-app traps and organized ambushes are a direct caution for trans visitors using apps.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: Court-based LGR with dead-name removal (2025) and publicly funded transition healthcare are resident-facing.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Security risks from the conflict (rockets, terrorism, border areas) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: First-person account of a transgender traveller's ordeal at the country's airport — security demanding surgery for gender recognition, documenting gender-identity humiliation at border screening.
News report (2025 data): homophobic and transphobic violence rose in the country during 2025 — official data showing an increase in anti-LGBTQ attacks.
News report: anti-LGBTQ violence hit a record high in the country — dating-app traps and organised ambushes luring victims to attacks; record assault totals.
News report: foreign inflammatory rhetoric is affecting the country's transgender community — foreign political discourse spilling into the local climate; local trans people report heightened fear.
News report: police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people — a protocol change after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees/travellers.
News report: registration of a person's previous name abolished for transgender people — a document-change policy removing old-name traceability.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying page addressed trans rights in the country — laws, protections and gaps.

Country at-a-glance profile by an international human-rights organisation (last updated 12 Mar 2026): no criminalization of consensual same-sex acts in the criminal code, some legal protections, but no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; baseline legal matrix.
A national survey found majority public support for same-sex marriage, while half of lawmakers declined to take a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 gender-identity law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. The capital is "one of the safest major cities for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the current government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the gender-identity law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, targeted searches). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the decrees.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010 (a first in the region) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a same-sex partner.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The decrees banning minors' hormone therapy and surgery, and the prison-housing decree, affect residents; the self-ID law, X marker and publicly funded transition healthcare are domestic administrative processes a visitor does not use.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General crime (robbery, scams) affects all tourists; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: Interviews (April 2025) with trans activists saying the president's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence; the situation described as 'chaotic, desperate'.

A national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

The government issued a decree modifying the gender-identity law as it pertains to minors, plus another decree on housing of transgender people in prisons; legal experts call the decree illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (Feb 2025) covers the country's decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors.

Overview by an international human-rights organisation (updated Mar 12, 2026): the country was the first in its region to legalise marriage equality (2010) and passed one of the world's most progressive gender-identity laws in 2012 allowing legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval; anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws — while the page's at-a-glance panel reports current negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration under review.

Commercial gay-travel safety guide (updated May 28, 2026): first-person account of walking the capital at every hour, giving practical gay-traveler safety impressions — useful as a recent on-the-ground visitor perspective.

Encyclopedia entry on the gender-identity law: approved by the lower legislative chamber by 167-17-7 and by the upper chamber on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated 24 May 2012; lauded as a pioneering step for transgender rights; allows legal gender change without surgery or court approval.

The supreme court left standing a life sentence for the murder of a trans activist, rejecting attempts to reinstate a gender-motivated-crime aggravating circumstance that an appellate court had removed in 2020 — meaning the aggravator is currently not applied.
rewrites.notes: Outlets, president, capital, organisations and case names omitted or genericised; 2010/2012 law dates, the 227-incident/62%/38-hour statistics and vote tallies retained; the regional 'first' comparator rendered 'first in the region'; a local identity term removed.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (trans women detained and denied entry at the airport), deported for having a male passport (a foreign trans model; a trans media personality), denied entry despite valid visas (a foreign trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (a foreign trans woman sentenced to one year). A foreign trans woman was arrested in her apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

The government "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "foreign tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, this country does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct, has no documented custodial death of a trans person, and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors travelling with a partner, or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Strict rules on social behaviour, drug possession, and financial crimes (exit bans) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: News report (2025): two trans women describe being detained for hours at the airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched their female passport records, mocked by staff, and denied entry with passports confiscated — a direct visitor-experience account of gender-document screening at entry.

News report (Mar 21, 2022): a foreign trans model was stopped at immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported before a scheduled appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

News report (Apr 2023): a foreign trans woman detained in the country since September 2022 — arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test — accused the consulate of negligence; a documented case of a trans foreigner in prolonged custody.

Legal review of the country: it employs various legal mechanisms that explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles; transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion — the legal-framework basis for visitor risk.

Country overview by an international human-rights organisation (last updated Mar 12, 2026): a new national criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (one provision also covers unmarried different-sex couples); charges require a complaint basis; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register.
News report (Aug 9, 2016): a trans media personality was denied entry and detained at the airport — an early high-profile case of a trans visitor refused entry on identity grounds.
rewrites.notes: Outlets, nationalities, names, venues and event names removed; sentence length and law dates retained; a banned statutory term rendered 'national criminal code'; article number dropped; the tourist-targeting demonym replaced with 'foreign tourists'.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country has one of the world's most progressive constitutional frameworks for trans rights — it was the first country to ban discrimination on sexual orientation (1996), has a legal gender recognition procedure (the 2003 sex-description act), marriage equality (2006), and an equality act prohibiting unfair discrimination on gender. The equality court recently ruled in favour of a trans inmate who was denied gender expression and healthcare in prison (November 2025), affirming the constitutional right to gender-affirming healthcare for inmates, and correctional services have developed a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners.

But there is a wide gap between law and lived reality. Legal gender recognition is administratively difficult, expensive, and inconsistently implemented. A trans woman was brutally attacked in a tavern (January 2025); a dating-app hostage ordeal was reported (December 2024); and anti-transgender violence has been documented within the public health system. There is a legal debate about whether businesses can refuse trans people facility access under the consumer protection act.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, private healthcare available, and its major cities have established queer scenes. The violence targets local trans communities, not tourists.
rewrites.blindTangential: The dating-app hostage ordeal (December 2024) is a caution for trans visitors using apps; the facility-access legal debate affects visitors' everyday exposure.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The legal gender recognition procedure under the 2003 sex-description act (difficult, expensive, inconsistently implemented) is resident-facing; the prison case and the public-health-system violence concern residents.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The country's high general crime rate (violent crime, carjackings, muggings) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: Full judgment (High Court, delivered ~14 Nov 2025): refusal to provide gender-affirming health care to a transgender inmate for whom it was prescribed falls below the required standard of health care; refusal to allow feminising clothing/accessories likewise impugned — binding equality-court remedies for detained trans persons.

Case summary (14 Nov 2025): the High Court sitting as an equality court ruled in favour of a transgender inmate against the correctional services department — ordering it to implement accommodations, enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates, and provide prescribed medical care.

Media statement (14 Nov 2025): welcomes the High Court ruling requiring correctional services to provide gender-affirming hormone treatment at public expense and to permit clothing/cosmetics expressing a trans woman's gender identity.

News report (6 Aug 2025): correctional services have a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners but rights organisations doubt implementation; a human-rights organisation represents a trans prisoner challenging conditions — pre-echo of the November 2025 equality court win.

Overview by an international human-rights organisation (updated Mar 2026): a marriage-equality law has been in force since 2006; since 2003 trans/intersex people can amend sex markers under the sex-description act (medical requirements pathologise identity; reform toward self-determination pending); a 2024 hate-crimes and hate-speech act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; violence disproportionately hits lesbian/trans/gender-nonconforming people.

Opinion piece (27 Jun 2025): ordinary administrative tasks are fraught with risk for trans people — medical requirements under the sex-description act lock people out of legal gender recognition, binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; a 2024 local report documents a trans woman denied filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID (police mockery).

News report (6 Jan 2025): a trans woman survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern on 26 Dec 2024, left with severe facial injuries and physical/emotional scars — she spoke out publicly; illustrates violent hate-crime risk against visible trans women in social venues.

Rights-watch report (Dec 2024): local activists spotlighted trans healthcare access — a memorandum to a hospital over year-long treatment delays; escalating hate violence with five LGBTQIA+ murders reported; also covers the tavern attack (arrest made).

Academic article (2024): analyses whether gender-segregated bathrooms to the exclusion of transgender/non-binary persons constitute unfair discrimination under consumer-protection law read with the constitutional equality clause — argues trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access; relevant to visitor facility anxiety.

Opinion piece (19 Jan 2026): makes the legal gender recognition case — mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and even arrest threats for 'fraud'; defines legal gender recognition as changing marker/name on official documents to align with identity; argues recognition should be a right grounded in dignity.

News report: the justice minister launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence, citing the constitution's equality clause — early (2010s-era) government recognition of LGBTI violence as a policy problem; historic context for the later hate-crimes act (2024).
rewrites.notes: Case parties, officials, bodies, outlets and place names omitted; law dates (1996/2003/2006/2024), ruling dates and statistics retained; the named sex-description act rendered generically; public-funding phrasing substituted for the funding wording of the source; unique quote, local settlement term and victim details removed.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented trans-traveler death in custody and a presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ as a national security threat. A foreign trans activist died in police custody in 2022 after arrest at an airport on his honeymoon (family alleges police beating; police deny violence).

In one province, Sharia law criminalises same-sex relations with public caning (applies to all persons in that province, including tourists). A new penal code effective January 2026 effectively criminalises all same-sex conduct nationally. The president in October 2025 classified "promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" as a national security threat alongside terrorism — and vigilante mob attacks on trans women escalated after this decree (10 attacks documented between March and July 2026). Police conduct discriminatory raids on gay gatherings (75 arrested in June 2025).

BUT: a major tourist hub exists where many trans visitors enter discreetly without incident; the country has no death penalty; and the death is disputed (police deny violence) rather than clearly documented torture.
rewrites.blindTangential: The new penal code (January 2026) criminalising all same-sex conduct nationally, and the province's Sharia caning provision (applying to tourists), are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Drug laws are severe (the activist was arrested on drug charges); general terrorism/crime risks in certain regions affect all travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (Aug 2022) covers police denying violence in the death of a foreign trans activist in custody.

Campus news report (Sept 2022): a university student from abroad on honeymoon was arrested at an airport on drug charges; on a messaging-app call his mother was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody, and his mother alleges police beat him — a documented death-in-custody case involving a trans traveler.

News report (14 August 2026): vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law — the president's October 2025 decree listing nonmilitary threats framed LGBTQ+ people within national defense policy. The report ties the violence and the official framing together as one escalation.

News report (15 August 2026): attacks on trans women 'did not suddenly appear' — analysis ties the surge to officials' latest verbal attacks and to the October 2025 presidential defense decree treating LGBT people as national-defense 'risks'. An academic commentator said the regulation shifts rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy — risks that must be monitored and controlled.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (Feb 2025) covers a province publicly caning two men for a same-sex relationship.

Country page by an international human-rights organisation (updated 12 March 2026): the country's new penal code took effect 2 January 2026 (signed December 2022) and penalises all consensual extra-marital sex between adults (reported as up to 2 years' imprisonment). Since same-sex marriage is not permitted, this effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with prosecution reported as selective — the current-law baseline for this record.

Country profile by an international human-rights organisation: two provinces of the country criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; national-level provisions target morality.

Report by an international human-rights organisation (June 2025): police raided a privately rented villa on Sunday 22 June 2025, arresting 75 people (74 men, 1 woman) after public reports of a 'gay party'. An official called it 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' and said the gathering violated no law — evidence of venue-based raids targeting LGBT gatherings.

Report by an international human-rights organisation (7 July 2026): has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in the country since 2016, following officials' condemnations of a student group at a university; a national LGBT umbrella organization documented 94 cases. Officials in early July called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

Report (10 August 2016): the national psychiatric association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities 'mental illnesses' and recommended psychological 'rehabilitation', while the then-government remained mostly silent — the origin point of the institutionalised anti-LGBT posture the record describes.
rewrites.notes: Names, university, cities, province names and outlet names omitted or genericised; dates and statistics (2022, 2025, 2026, 10, 75, 94) retained; the torture reference kept without the government qualifier; app and venue names genericised.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a dangerous destination for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the historic-era penal code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe, and 25 trans and intersex people told an international news outlet this kind of police harassment is "common." The national human rights commission's report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist was murdered — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, this country's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a transgender protection rights bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered transgender protection rights bill is a positive trajectory.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, applies to tourists) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The court-ordered transgender protection rights bill and the 2026 LGR ruling are resident-facing developments; the eviction/arrest/mob-violence toll falls on residents.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Terrorism risks near the border, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: Government policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

International news feature on trans and intersex people: 26 interviewees describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion (demands for cash), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Report (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in the country, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges a 2019 High Court ruling that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

Press release: a High Court handed transgender people a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the government to enact a transgender protection rights act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans person subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

Report on a High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026: follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse people were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; the country has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (Dec 2024) covers a man sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

Country profile by an international human-rights organisation (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 an appeals court ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

News report (23 Sep 2025) on the national human rights commission's report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite the constitutional dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

Human rights report (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 local religious leaders demanded closure of an HIV research institute.
rewrites.notes: Names, cities, outlets, statute proper names and the currency reference removed or genericised; counts (102/43/25/50/26/94) and ruling dates retained; the penal code's era descriptor rendered 'historic-era'; the border-country reference rendered 'the border'; unique murder-case detail removed.
